transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for having me. I, um... well, I came in because I just feel completely worn out almost every single day. And I don't really get it, because it's not like I'm staying up all night or anything. I'll get a full night's sleep, eight hours, sometimes even nine if I make a point to go to bed early, but when I wake up, it's like... it's like my body didn't get the memo. 

My body and my head are just completely dragging. I work as a cashier, and when my alarm goes off for my shift, I just sit there on the edge of the mattress and my whole body feels like lead. It takes everything I have just to put my work shirt on. You'd think ringing up groceries isn't the most demanding thing in the world, and I mean, it's not, I've been doing it a while and I know it's not, but lately just the thought of standing there at the register... I'm just so tired. Every day, just this heavy, dragging feeling in my brain and my bones before the day even starts, no matter how much rest I try to get.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?

Well, yeah, I mean... I still like doing my normal stuff. It's not like I'm just sitting in a dark room staring at the wall or anything. Like, for example, I'm a big baseball guy. I've been following the Braves since I was in middle school, and I still love watching the games. I have this whole routine where I get my snacks set up, sit in my specific spot on the couch—it's this old recliner I got a few years back, but it's super comfortable—and I still get really into the game, you know? Yelling at the screen if the umpire makes a bad call, texting my buddy Dave about the plays. I still get a kick out of all that. 

And I play some video games, too, mostly sports ones or sometimes those big open-world ones, and I still have fun doing that. I still want to do those things, and when I'm doing them, I'm having a good time. It's not that I don't care anymore or lost the taste for it. 

It's really just what I was saying a minute ago about being so drained. Like, I still enjoy the baseball game completely, but lately I might just accidentally fall asleep in the third inning because my eyes are so heavy, and then I wake up at 2 AM and the TV is just showing infomercials. And that really bugs me, because then I have to check my phone in the morning to see who won, which totally ruins the suspense of watching it live, you know? You want to see the walk-off hit when it happens, not read a little box score the next day while you're brushing your teeth. But the actual enjoyment part? Yeah, that's all still there. I definitely still like my hobbies.
Do you often feel sad or down for most of the day?

Sad? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I don't feel depressed or down in the dumps or anything like that. It's not like... well, okay, my buddy Dave, right? A couple of years ago he went through this really rough patch when his dog passed away—this big golden retriever named Buster, really great dog, used to actually bring him the mail and everything—and Dave was just devastated. He was genuinely sad. Like, he wouldn't leave his apartment, just sitting there looking at old photos on his phone, crying. That's what I think of when someone says sad. 

But for me, it's not like that at all. I don't have that, you know, that dark cloud hanging over my head. I'm not weeping in the breakroom at the grocery store or feeling hopeless or anything. My mood is actually pretty okay, all things considered. I mean, sure, I get frustrated. I get *really* frustrated, actually, because, like I was just saying, I'm just so tired all the time. And who wouldn't be annoyed when you're dragging your feet all day and missing the end of a good baseball game because you couldn't keep your eyes open? It drives me absolutely crazy. 

But being annoyed or frustrated isn't the same as being sad. I'm actually pretty content with things overall. I like my apartment, I've got my routine, I don't even mind the cashier job most days, except for when it gets super busy right before a holiday. Like Thanksgiving, people go absolutely nuts over canned cranberry sauce, I swear, it's like they've never seen it before. But yeah, no, definitely not sad. Just... just completely worn out, and maybe a little irritated that I'm so worn out. But not sad.
Have you noticed any change in your weight recently?

Weight? No, I don't think so. I mean, I wear the same uniform pants to work every day. We have these dark blue, sort of khaki-material pants we have to wear at the register, and they still fit exactly the same as they did a year ago. I actually bought a new belt a few months ago, this brown leather one from Target, because my old one was starting to fray right around the buckle, and I'm still on the exact same notch. The third hole from the end. So, physically, I'm pretty sure I'm sitting right around the same weight I've been for the last five or six years. 

I don't really own a scale at home to check it exactly. Well, I used to, but it was one of those cheap digital ones where the battery died and I just never bothered to figure out which of those little flat coin batteries it needed to replace it, you know? But my appetite is totally normal. Working at the grocery store, you see food all day long, so I just grab my usual deli sandwich on my lunch break—usually turkey and provolone on wheat, maybe a small bag of barbecue chips if I'm feeling it—and I eat exactly like I always have. So yeah, no weight gain or loss or anything like that. Just the same old me, just... really, really tired all the time, like I was saying before. But no, the weight is definitely steady.
Do you have trouble focusing or paying attention to things?

Well, yeah, actually, I have been having some trouble with that. It's... it's kind of embarrassing, honestly, because my job really isn't that complicated. I mean, you scan the items, you bag them, you take the money. I've been doing it long enough that it should be pure muscle memory, right? But lately, I'll be standing there at the register, and I can be looking right at the screen, right at the total, and I just completely lose track of what I'm doing. 

It's like my brain just drifts off. I'll start thinking about, I don't know, whether I remembered to lock the deadbolt on my apartment door, or if I paid the electric bill—which, by the way, they just raised the rates again, which is a whole other thing to worry about—and suddenly the customer is just standing there staring at me, holding out a twenty-dollar bill, and I have to kind of snap back to reality. And because I spaced out, that's when I end up making a stupid mistake, like hitting the wrong button for the change or forgetting to scan a coupon they handed me. 

Then I have to call the manager over to do an override, which holds up the whole line, and people start sighing and looking at their watches. It's the worst feeling. And then at the end of the shift, I end up having to recount my drawer because I'm paranoid I messed up the cash, which just keeps me there longer when all I want to do is go home and sleep because I'm so exhausted. It's just... my mind is always going a million miles an hour about everything else except what's right in front of me, you know? So, yeah, focusing has definitely been a bit of a struggle lately.
Have you had periods in the past where you didn't feel this tired and struggled to focus less?

Oh, yeah, absolutely. I mean, I wasn't always like this. I used to be pretty sharp, honestly. I could ring up a whole cart of groceries, chat with the customer about the weather or whatever, and bag everything perfectly without even breaking a sweat. I had a lot more energy back then, too. I'd actually go out after work sometimes, maybe grab a beer with Dave or just stay up watching a movie instead of passing out on the couch at 8 PM. 

But this whole... whatever this is, being so exhausted and my brain just feeling like it's full of static all the time, it really started, let's see... it's been about a year and three months now. Yeah, almost exactly. Because that's when my older relative—my aunt, actually—moved in with us. She had a fall, nothing broken, thank God, but she just couldn't live on her own anymore, and the assisted living places are just so unbelievably expensive, you know? Like, thousands of dollars a month, which is insane. So she moved into our spare room. 

And don't get me wrong, I love her, she's family, but man, it completely flipped my life upside down. Suddenly there's all these extra things to worry about, like making sure she took her pills, and the house has to be quiet at certain times, and she watches the TV at top volume—she loves those old game shows, like the really old episodes of The Price is Right with Bob Barker, which is fine, but it's just constant noise. And ever since she got settled in, I just... I haven't been the same. It's just been this non-stop drain on my energy and my focus. So, yeah, before a year and three months ago, I was totally fine. Just a regular guy doing his job. Now, it's just a struggle every single day.
Do you wake up feeling rested after a full night's sleep?

Rested? No, not really. Honestly, I don't think I've woken up feeling actually rested in... well, probably since my aunt moved in, like I was saying. It's just so frustrating because I'll get into bed, right? And I'm exhausted. My legs are aching from standing at the register all day, my eyes are heavy, and all I want to do is just crash. I even bought these nice new pillows from Bed Bath & Beyond before they closed down, the memory foam ones with the cooling gel on one side, thinking maybe that would help. But it doesn't matter. 

The second my head hits that cooling gel, it's like a switch flips in my brain. I just lie there staring at the ceiling, and my mind starts running through this massive checklist. I start thinking about the bills—like that electric bill I mentioned, and whether I remembered to transfer money from savings to checking to cover the water bill, which is due on the 14th. Then I start stressing about my work schedule for the next week, wondering if my manager scheduled me for a closing shift followed by an opening shift again, which they call a "clopen," and it's just brutal. And then I start worrying about everyone at home, you know? Like, is my aunt comfortable? Did she remember to lock the back door after she let the dog out? What if she gets up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom and trips over the rug in the hallway? I should probably tape that rug down tomorrow. 

And it just goes on and on like that for hours. I'll look over at the alarm clock, and it'll be 1:00 AM, then 2:30 AM. And even when I finally do manage to drift off, it's not a deep sleep. It's this really light, restless kind of sleep where I'm tossing and turning, tangling up the sheets. When the alarm finally goes off at 6:00 AM, I feel like I never even really settled down. I drag myself out of bed feeling just as tired, if not more tired, than when I went to sleep. It's like my body was resting, but my brain was pulling a double shift all night. So no, definitely not waking up feeling rested. Not at all.
Do you think the racing thoughts at night are causing you to not feel rested in the morning?

Oh, a hundred percent. That's exactly it. Because it's not like I'm just lying there trying to solve one single problem, where I can just figure it out and go to sleep. It feels like my mind is always jumping from one thing to the next, just non-stop. Like a pinball machine, you know? 

I'll start off worrying about money, trying to figure out how to stretch my paycheck to cover all these rising costs, and then bam, my brain jumps to the relative staying with us—my aunt—and how much the dynamic in the house has changed since she took over the spare room. And then, of course, that makes me think about my wife, because she has been so incredibly stressed out lately trying to help manage things with my aunt and the house, and I hate seeing her so overwhelmed, it just makes me feel terrible and guilty. 

And then, out of nowhere, before I even finish feeling guilty about my wife, I'm suddenly stressing over my church duties! I help out with setting up the fellowship hall on Sundays and organizing the food pantry donations, and I'll be lying in bed at 3 AM terrified I forgot to sign up for the cleanup crew or that I'm going to oversleep and let Pastor Dave down. And then, naturally, worrying about oversleeping makes me start panicking about whether I'm messing up at work, like making those stupid mistakes on the register that I told you about, giving back the wrong change or holding up the line. 

It's just... it's exhausting. Money, my aunt, my wife being stressed, church stuff, work... it just loops and loops and loops. I'll fixate on one thing for ten minutes, and then my brain just tosses another worry onto the pile. So, yeah, the racing thoughts are absolutely why I feel like garbage in the morning. My body might be in the bed, but my brain literally never turns off to actually get any rest.
Do you often feel guilty about things that have happened or things you've done?

Guilty? I mean, I wouldn't say I feel guilty about things I've done, no. Not really. It's more like... I worry about things that *could* happen or things I *might* mess up, like I was just saying with work and church. But actual guilt over things in the past? No, I don't think so. I try to be a good person, you know? I show up to work on time, I help out at the church, I do my best to support my wife and my aunt. I've never done anything terrible that keeps me up at night feeling remorseful, if that's what you mean. 

Sure, I feel bad when my wife is stressed, but that's just because I care about her and I hate seeing her overwhelmed with everything going on in the house. It's not like I feel guilty because I did something specific to cause it, it's just the situation, you know? The situation with my aunt moving in and the bills and everything. It's just a lot of pressure. But yeah, no, I don't sit around feeling guilty about past mistakes or anything like that. My brain is too busy worrying about what's going to happen tomorrow to really dwell on what happened yesterday, if that makes sense. Honestly, I wish I could just turn off the worrying about tomorrow, because that's the real problem. The past is the past, you know? I can't change it, so I don't really beat myself up over it. It's the future that really gets to me.
Are you finding it harder to do your daily tasks or maintain your relationships because of how you're feeling?

Yeah, actually, I really am. It's... it's getting tough. Like at work, for instance. I've been having to double-check my cash drawer so much more often lately because I just keep making these small mistakes. I mean, usually, I'm pretty quick at the register. I've been doing this a long time, so you get a rhythm, right? Scan, bag, take the cash, make change, wish them a good day. But lately, because my brain is just so fried from not sleeping and worrying about everything at home, the rhythm is completely gone. 

I'll hand back three singles instead of four, or I'll stare at a twenty-dollar bill and for a second my brain just completely blanks on the basic math. So now, I'm constantly stopping to recount the drawer. I'll count the fives, then second-guess myself, and count them again just to be absolutely sure I didn't mess up. It slows down my line, which makes the customers start huffing and puffing and looking at their watches, and then I get even more stressed out about holding them up. My manager hasn't formally written me up or anything yet, but I know she's noticing that I'm slower and a little scattered.

And then outside of work, it's definitely affecting things too. Like with the church stuff I mentioned earlier. I've actually had to cut back on my volunteering at the food pantry. I just... I don't feel like I can keep up with everything anymore. It used to be something I really looked forward to, you know? Sorting the canned goods, checking the expiration dates, making up the boxes for the families that come in on Tuesdays. It felt good to help out. But now, just the thought of adding one more thing to my schedule makes my chest feel tight. 

I had to pull Pastor Dave aside last week and tell him that I can't do every Saturday anymore, that I need to step back. I felt awful doing it, I really did, but I'm just so drained by the time the weekend hits. I just don't have the energy or the focus to organize the donations properly. So between the register mistakes and having to step back from the pantry, I just feel like I'm dropping the ball everywhere. It's like I'm constantly running on fumes and I just can't keep all the plates spinning like I used to.
Are you having trouble maintaining relationships with friends and family due to your current state?

Well, like I was saying, it's definitely putting a strain on things, you know? With my wife, she's already so stressed with her own stuff, and my aunt being there, and I feel like I'm not bringing my A-game to the relationship because I'm just so drained. I come home and I'm just shot. I don't have the energy to really sit and talk or go out and do things with her like we used to, because my brain is just spinning from the day. 

And friends... honestly, I haven't really been seeing them much at all. I mean, my main social circle is mostly through the church anyway, right? The guys I do the food pantry with, we usually grab a coffee or breakfast after we finish sorting the donations on Saturday mornings. We'd sit at the diner for like an hour, just catching up on the week, talking about sports or whatever. It was a good time. But since I've had to cut back on volunteering, like I mentioned, I'm missing out on that time with them. I just don't have it in me to go down there and do the heavy lifting and the organizing, and then sit around and try to be social when all I want to do is go home and try to get some rest, even though I know I probably won't sleep anyway. 

It's just... it feels like everything is slipping a little bit. Work is harder because of the mistakes with the register and constantly having to recount the drawer to make sure I'm not messing up the change. And then my free time, which used to be for friends and helping out, is just gone because I'm too exhausted. So yeah, I guess you could say my relationships are definitely taking a hit because I just can't keep up with everything the way I used to. I feel like I'm just barely keeping my head above water with work and the house, and there's nothing left over for anyone else.
Have your feelings of tiredness and difficulty focusing been constant since they started, or have they been varying in intensity?

Well, I mean, it's pretty much constant now, but it didn't start out that way, you know? It’s been… gosh, I’d say it’s been going on for about a year and three months now. Yeah, right around then. That’s when my aunt—my wife’s aunt, actually, but we just call her my aunt—that's when she moved in with us. Before that, I mean, sure, I’d get tired after a long shift at the store, especially if it was near the holidays and the lines were crazy, but this… this is different. 

When she first moved in, it was just an adjustment period, right? We were trying to figure out the new routine, moving furniture around, making space for her things. So the tiredness back then just felt like normal stress. But then, as the months went on, it just never went away. It settled in. And the focus thing, that really started creeping up on me. I’d be standing at the register, and instead of just ringing up the groceries, my mind would be completely back at the house—wondering if my aunt remembered to take her pills, or if my wife was getting overwhelmed trying to cook dinner while dealing with her. 

And it hasn't let up. It’s like a hum in the background all the time. From the minute I wake up—if I even slept—to the minute I lay down, I'm just drained. Some days might feel a tiny bit better if work is slow and I don't have to interact with as many people, but the baseline is just… exhausted. And the brain fog is always there. It’s been a solid fifteen months of just feeling like I’m walking through molasses, physically and mentally. It hasn't really come and gone, it just started when she moved in and slowly got to the point where it’s just my everyday reality now.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in most activities?

Depressed? Um, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know I just talked a lot about stepping back from the food pantry and not seeing the guys at the diner, and I guess that probably sounds like I'm losing interest in things, but it's really not that at all. It's not that I don't *want* to do those things. I actually really miss doing them. Like, on Saturday mornings now, I'll be sitting in the kitchen, just staring at my coffee mug while my aunt is watching her morning shows, and I'll look at the clock and think, 'Oh, they're probably just finishing up the canned goods right now, they're probably heading over to the diner to grab a booth.' And I really wish I was there with them. I still have the interest, you know? It's just that I'm so physically and mentally drained from worrying about everything at the house and trying not to mess up my drawer at work that I just can't bring myself to actually go and be social. 

So it's definitely not a lack of interest. And as for feeling depressed... no, I don't think I've ever had a couple of weeks where I just felt flat-out depressed or down in the dumps like that. Because, the way I see it, if you're depressed, you kind of stop caring, right? You just sort of give up and check out. But my problem is almost the exact opposite. I care way too much about every little thing. My brain is constantly going, just spinning and spinning about the cash register, or my aunt's routine, or my wife getting too stressed out. If I was depressed, maybe I wouldn't be so wound up all the time. But I'm just constantly on edge, just waiting for the next ball to drop. So, no, I haven't really had that feeling of just being depressed and not caring. It's always just been this overwhelming feeling of trying to keep up with all the worry and just running completely out of gas.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past year?

Weight? Um, no, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, my clothes still fit the same as they always have. I've been wearing the same work khakis for, gosh, probably three years now, and I haven't had to buy a new belt or anything. I guess if I think about it, my eating habits haven't really changed all that much either. Even with everything going on, with my aunt moving in and the stress at the store and just feeling exhausted all the time... we still try to have dinner together. My wife usually cooks, or sometimes we just throw something easy in the oven if we're both too tired, like a frozen lasagna or something. 

Actually, if anything, I might be eating a little more of the junk stuff when I'm stressed. You know how it is, you get home and you're just so keyed up, sometimes you just want a handful of chips or a cookie while you're trying to wind down in front of the TV. But no, I haven't stepped on a scale recently, but just going by how I feel and how my clothes fit, I definitely haven't lost a significant amount of weight. It's funny you ask, though, because sometimes I feel like I'm running around so much in my own head that I should be burning a million calories a day just from worrying, but I guess it doesn't really work like that, does it? So yeah, my weight has been pretty steady, right around where it usually is. No big changes there.
Are there any daily activities that you've had to stop doing altogether because of your tiredness and difficulty focusing?

Well, stop doing *altogether*? I don't know if I've completely stopped everything, but I've definitely had to pull back a lot. I mean, I think I mentioned the food pantry earlier. I used to volunteer there every Saturday morning, sorting cans, helping load boxes... it was a good routine. But I've really had to cut back on that. I haven't been in weeks. It's just... by the time Saturday rolls around, I'm so incredibly drained, and my brain is just buzzing with all the things I need to do at the house, or worrying about my aunt, that I just don't feel like I can keep up with everything there. It feels like too much to manage, you know? Like if I go, I'll just be standing there staring at a box of green beans, completely zoned out, and I won't actually be any help to anyone.

And at work—I haven't stopped working, obviously, I need the job—but the way I do things has had to change. The focus thing is really messing with me there. I'm a cashier, right? So it's a lot of rapid-fire transactions, especially when it gets busy. Lately, I've had to start double-checking my cash drawer constantly. Like, way more often than I used to. I’ll be handing someone their change, and suddenly I’ll freeze, thinking, 'Wait, did they hand me a twenty or a fifty? Did I just give them back a ten instead of a five?' I've made a couple of small mistakes recently, just stupid little errors because my mind was drifting off to whether my wife remembered to pick up my aunt's prescription, and it really rattled me. So now I'm constantly recounting the bills, slowing down the line, just trying to make absolutely sure my drawer isn't short at the end of my shift. It's exhausting having to second-guess myself all day long like that. So yeah, I haven't stopped working, but I'm definitely not functioning the way I used to.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in most activities, and if so, did it include a time when you felt that way almost every day?

Um, didn't you just ask me that? About being depressed? I'm pretty sure we just talked about that a minute ago, right? Because, like I said, I wouldn't really use the word depressed for what I'm going through. It's not that heavy, you know, 'I can't get out of bed, I don't care about anything' kind of feeling. I mean, my wife had an uncle who got really depressed after he lost his job at the auto plant a few years back, and he just sat in his recliner all day watching old westerns and wouldn't even answer the phone. He just completely checked out. And that's not me at all. 

I care. I care a lot. Probably too much, to be honest. That's the whole problem. I'm just so wound up and anxious about the cash drawer at work, and my aunt's situation at home, and just trying to keep all the plates spinning, that I get totally exhausted. And yeah, because I'm so tired and my brain won't shut off, I haven't been going to the food pantry on Saturdays, and I miss seeing the guys at the diner. But the interest is still there. I still want to do those things. I'm just too wiped out from all the worrying to actually go do them. So, no, I haven't had a two-week period where I felt depressed or lost interest every day. It's just... it's just the worry that's draining me, not depression. I'm pretty sure I already explained all that, though, didn't I?
Have you ever had a period where you felt depressed or lost interest in activities that lasted for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Wait, I'm sorry, didn't you just ask me that exact same thing? Like, just a second ago? Because I really feel like I just answered this. I mean, I don't want to be difficult or anything, but I'm pretty sure we just went over this whole depression thing. Like I was just saying about my wife's uncle, the one who worked at the auto plant—he was depressed. He had that thing where he just completely shut down and wouldn't even look at the TV sometimes, just stared at the wall. That's not what's happening with me. 

I don't have those two-week periods where I'm just down in the dumps all day, every day, not caring about anything. It's actually the complete opposite. I care about everything all the time, and it never stops. I'm constantly thinking about whether I messed up at work, or if my aunt is okay at the house while my wife is busy, or if I forgot to pay the electric bill. It's just this constant hum of worry in the background of my head, from the minute I wake up until I finally manage to fall asleep, which takes forever anyway. So no, I really don't feel depressed or like I've lost interest in things. I still want to do stuff, I'm just too exhausted from all the worrying to actually do it. So yeah, like I said before, no to the depression thing. I just... I really feel like we just covered this. Are you sure you didn't just ask me that?
Have you felt tired, had trouble focusing, or experienced any other symptoms we've discussed for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks at any point?

Oh, yeah, absolutely. It's been way longer than two weeks. I mean, it feels like it's just my normal now, which is pretty frustrating, to be honest. If I really think back on it, trying to pinpoint exactly when this whole... this whole cycle of being exhausted and not being able to focus and just worrying constantly started... it really goes back to about a year and three months ago. 

That's when my wife's aunt moved in with us. Before that, you know, things were pretty standard. We had our routine, I went to work, came home, we'd watch TV or I'd go volunteer... it was manageable. But then her aunt's health started declining, and she couldn't live on her own anymore. We didn't want to put her in a home—my wife was really against that, and I get it, family is family—so we cleared out the spare room, the one we used to just keep the ironing board and my old guitar in, and moved her in. 

And man, ever since then, it's just been this constant, low-grade stress that never really goes away. It's like my brain just shifted into overdrive and forgot how to shift back down. So yeah, for the last year and three months, pretty much every single day, for most of the day, I'm just dragging. I wake up tired, I go to work tired, I'm second-guessing myself at the register, I come home tired, and then I just sit there worrying about whether we're doing enough for her, or if the medical bills are going to pile up, or if I'm going to mess up at work because I can't concentrate. So it's definitely been way, way longer than a couple of weeks. It's been well over a year of this every day.
Have you felt this way for at least two weeks?

Wait, didn't you just... I mean, I feel like we just covered this, didn't we? Like, literally just a second ago? Because I was just saying, it's been way, way longer than two weeks. Two weeks would be a breeze compared to this. No, it's been about a year and three months. 

I know exactly when it started because, like I was just explaining, that's when my wife's aunt had to move into our spare room. It was right around the end of the summer, a year ago last summer, because I remember we had to move the window AC unit out of that room so she wouldn't get a draft. And ever since we got her settled in there, it's just been this non-stop feeling of being drained and worried. Every single day. So, yeah, it's definitely been at least two weeks. It's been a year and three months of feeling like this, day in and day out. I really thought I just said all that, though?
Have you felt this way for at least two weeks?

Okay, now I'm starting to actually worry that maybe I'm not explaining myself right, or maybe I'm doing this whole interview wrong? Because you literally just asked me that. I mean, word for word, you just asked if I've felt this way for at least two weeks. And I just said yes, but way, way longer—a year and three months. 

Did you not hear me, or is this like... some kind of psychological test to see if my memory is working, or if I'll change my answer? Because I'm already stressed enough as it is, you know, with work and the house, and feeling like I have to repeat myself over and over is just making me more anxious. Like I was just saying, it's been about 15 months. If you do the math—and I'm on a register all day, so I do a lot of math in my head—15 months is roughly 60 weeks. So yes, absolutely, 100 percent, 60 weeks is at least two weeks. It's been happening every single day since my wife's aunt moved into our spare room. I just... I really don't know how else to say it. Do you need me to explain the timeline differently? Because I feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit here answering the exact same question again.
